title: Caroline Mueni's Toilet and the First Day of Sanergy's Fresh Life
dek: On World Toilet Day 2011 a Mukuru grocer became the first resident to run a Fresh Life toilet, the start of Sanergy's bet on franchising sanitation.

story.founder: David Auerbach, Ani Vallabhaneni, Lindsay Stradley (with co-founders Nathan Cooke and Joel Veenstra)
story.event: Building the first Fresh Life toilets in Mukuru and franchising them to residents
story.summary: Sanergy, started by MIT business students including David Auerbach, Lindsay Stradley and Ani Vallabhaneni, built trial toilets in Kibera and Mukuru, won MIT's $100K competition in 2011 and moved to Mukuru, Nairobi. On World Toilet Day, 19 November 2011, Caroline Mueni became its first Fresh Life Operator, running a franchised toilet whose waste Sanergy collected and turned into fertiliser. The network passed 100 toilets in 2012 and reached 615 by 2015, short of its target of 1,000.
paragraphs: On World Toilet Day, 19 November 2011, Caroline Mueni, who ran a small grocery stand in Mukuru kwa Njenga in Nairobi, became the first person to run a Fresh Life toilet for Sanergy. She paid for it from her savings. Her neighbours were getting sick, David Auerbach later wrote, and her children had to walk more than 100 metres through unsafe areas to reach community toilets. The toilet was a concrete cubicle three feet by five, with sealed containers under the floor for a Sanergy crew to empty.

The idea began in 2009 in a class at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where Auerbach, Lindsay Stradley and Ani Vallabhaneni, all business students, were asked to design ventures for problems faced by a billion people or more; MIT also counts Nathan Cooke and Joel Veenstra as co-founders. Research in Nairobi showed them that pay toilets already existed, but they were built so that waste could not be collected regularly, and the people running them struggled to make a profit. "We saw a broken sanitation value chain," Auerbach said.

With about $25,000 from MIT's Public Service Center, the team built two trial toilets, one in Kibera and one in Mukuru, and a rough system for turning waste into fertiliser. In 2011 the plan won MIT's $100K business plan competition. The choice they made was to sell toilets to residents, with training, branding and daily waste collection included, and to earn Sanergy's own money from what the waste became. Operators set their own prices and kept the takings; "their success is their own," Stradley said. A few months later the company moved to Mukuru.

A second toilet followed in December. By September 2012, when the lending site Kiva began financing would-be operators, VOA counted 86 toilets run by 50 entrepreneurs; Stradley put it at about 100. The founders aimed for 1,000 by 2015. An MIT Sloan case records 615 by then and growth goals missed, and some operators struggled for customers or defaulted on loans. On World Toilet Day 2014, Auerbach wrote, Caroline Mueni bought two more toilets.

quote.text: be content if the smallest thing goes on well, and consider such an event to be no small matter.
quote.source_title: Thoughts of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, tr. George Long, Project Gutenberg eBook #15877
quote.connection: Marcus, writing to himself, warns against waiting for an ideal state before acting. Sanergy's founders were aiming at a citywide problem, but their work began with one woman's toilet beside her grocery stand, and three years later she was buying two more.

reflection: Sanergy's plan was large: a whole chain from toilet to fertiliser across Nairobi's settlements. Its first day was small: one toilet, one operator. The target of a thousand toilets by 2015 was missed, and the 615 that stood by then still served tens of thousands of people.

You will set targets you do not reach, in your work and outside it. Marcus does not ask you to stop aiming. He asks you to count the smaller thing that went well as no small matter, rather than letting the missed number erase it. That is not settling for less. It is keeping an honest record.
invitation: Write down one small thing that went well this week, in your work or at home. Put it where you will see it tomorrow morning, beside the larger goal it belongs to.

cross_checks.claim: The first franchised Fresh Life toilet opened on World Toilet Day in November 2011
Sanergy grew out of an MIT class and won the 2011 MIT $100K competition after trial toilets in Kibera and Mukuru
The decision: franchise toilets to residents who run them as businesses while Sanergy collects and processes the waste
By September 2012 there were about 86 to 100 toilets, with Kiva financing operators
The target was 1,000 toilets by 2015; 615 had been franchised by 2015

research_notes: Founders: the slate and the MIT Sloan and Berkeley cases name three co-founders (Auerbach, Stradley, Vallabhaneni); MIT News names five, adding Nathan Cooke (a former D-Lab instructor) and Joel Veenstra; Business Daily names four including Cooke; the Daily Beast says five. The story names the three and notes MIT's other two. First toilet date: Stradley (NextBillion 2012), the Guardian (2012) and Auerbach (HuffPost 2014) say the first franchised toilet opened on World Toilet Day in November 2011; a June 2012 SOIL blog post says 28 toilets had been installed 'since the first was installed in November 2010', which probably refers to the trial toilets MIT News describes before the 2011 $100K win; the story uses the founders' 2011 date and mentions the trials separately. Global Press Journal says Sanergy was founded in July 2011. Counts in 2012 differ: SOIL (June) 28 in Mukuru; VOA (September) 86 toilets for 50 entrepreneurs; Stradley (NextBillion, around the September 2012 Clinton Global Initiative) about 100; the Guardian (November) over 100. Both September figures are given with attribution. Later counts: MIT News early 2014, 330 toilets and about 170 operators; Daily Beast 365 and 190; Auerbach November 2014, 575 and 274; MIT Sloan case, 615 by 2015 serving about 32,000 people with 2015 growth goals missed. The story uses the Sloan figure against the 1,000 target that both the Guardian and the Daily Beast report. The $100K win is dated 2011 (MIT News, the Sloan case and CMR); the month is not stated in a loaded source, so none is given. Caroline Mueni's story rests on Auerbach's own HuffPost guest post and is attributed to him. The physical description of the toilet is from Stradley's 2012 interview. The quote is Marcus Aurelius's note to himself about not waiting for an ideal commonwealth; the excerpt begins after a footnote marker in the Gutenberg text.
